Mugabe Endgame?

By: Graham Coetzer | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
As reports surfaced about a possible coup in Zimbabwe on tuesday night, we probe the situation in South Africa's notorious neighbour

Unique Selling Point:
Coup or a test of Zimbabwe's President Robert Mugabe's authority? As reports reached South African shores on tuesday night of explosions and a possible takeover of the national broadcaster on tuesday night, many Zimbabweans citizens took to social media, uploading videos of tank convoys and military vehicles seen near Mugabe's home.

Summary:
The army have taken control of Harare but in a video statement denied a coup. Meanwhile President Zuma has said President Mugabe is being confined to his home but in good condition. President Zuma is sending the SA ministers of defence and state security to Zim to meet with Mugabe. It seems Mugabe's ailing health has created a power vacuum, and vying for the top job is Grace Mugabe and sacked vice president Emmerson Mnangagwa.

Press Release:


Zimbabwe: A New Dawn?
As soldiers patrol the streets of Harare, taking over the state broadcaster ZBC, the ruling party Zanu-PF
continues to deny reports of a military takeover in Zimbabwe. Meanwhile, hope is rising that the country
may finally see long-awaited change. Carte Blanche gets in-depth analysis on these political developments.

Script:


Zimbabwe: A New Dawn?

Voice
Once revered by his people as a freedom fighter and liberation leader, Zimbabwean President Robert Gabriel Mugabe personified the African anti-colonial struggle. Sadly, the dream didn’t last and Zimbabwe suffered a dismal decline to one of the world’s poorest countries that caused a mass exodus of its people. (20s05f)
Link John
On Tuesday news hit South Africa of armored personnel carriers rumbling onto the streets of Harare. The Zimbabwean military avoided calling it a coup, but the impact was exactly the same. Toppling Robert Mugabe as the country’s long serving president. But if that was the beginning, the question now becomes, what is the endgame?
Voice
Zimbabweans took to social media, posting images and videos as the army seized power. Rumors of key ZANU-PF members’ arrests were rife, and reports indicated the military had captured the state broadcaster ZBC and were keeping the president under house arrest. Then on Wednesday, Zimbabwe’s Major General SB Moyo appeared on national television.(23s02f)
Sound Up SB Moyo
Comrade Robert G Mugabe and his family are safe and sound and their security is guaranteed. We are only targeting criminals around him, who are committing crimes that are causing social and economic suffering in the country in order to bring them to justice.
Voice
It soon became apparent that the military were in absolute control, with even ardent Mugabe regime supporters like Kudzai Chipanga, leader of the powerful ZANU-PF youth wing, apologizing for belittling the defense forces chief, General Constantino Chiwenga.(17s06f)
Sound Up Kudzai Chipanga
I kindly request General Chiwenga to please accept my apologies on behalf of the youth league and myself. We are still young people, we are still growing up. We learn from our mistakes.

Voice
Deputy Public Protector Advocate Kevin Malunga is a Zimbabwean by birth, and says he remembers a very different country to the one we know today. (8s22f)
Sound Up Kevin Malunga
I was born into a very prosperous Zimbabwe. A Zimbabwe where everything worked. There was a fully functional education system, a very strong health care system. A sense of accountability, the courts worked, the stock exchange worked. And it was a model, a model of excellence on the African continent. Also known as the breadbasket of Africa.
Voice
But under Mugabe’s rule things changed, as farm evictions, election violence and a dramatically devalued currency brought Africa’s breadbasket to it’s knees. (10s19f)
Sound Up Kevin Malunga
So I get a sense that many people are nostalgic, even myself, for those days.
Link John
It didn’t take long for attention to turn to Jacob Zuma. He called for an emergency SADC meeting, which took place in Botswana. And immediately dispatched to Zimbabwe a high level delegation led by the ministers of defense and state security.
Sound Up Jacob Zuma
Given the seriousness of the situation, I’ve taken a decision to send an envoy to be able to contact the leaders of the defense force who have undertaken these operations, but also to meet with president Mugabe.
Voice
On Thursday the first images of Mugabe since his house arrest emerged. Significantly, he has not been allowed to address the nation, and speculation is rife about the nature of the negotiations behind closed doors. Former Associate Professor of Development Studies at the University of Zimbabwe Brian Raftopoulos says we are witnessing the results of a ZANU-PF interparty power struggle. (25s03f)

Sound Up Brian Raftopoulos
John: So this is a classic power vacuum coup, it’s about people entrenching their own positions?
Brian: I think that it’s clearly an intervention on the behalf of one faction within ZANU-PF. And that’s the bottom line; they’ve intervened on behalf of Emmerson Mnangagwa. And they’re casting it as a national solution, but it is definitely an intra-party fight within ZANU-PF.
Voice
The dramatic turn in Robert Mugabe’s fortunes this week started on the 6th of November, when he fired Vice President Emmerson Mnangagwa. Nicknamed “Ngwena” or “The Crocodile” because of his ruthlessness, the 75-year-old has strong ties to Zimbabwe’s defense establishment. Many commentators believe Mugabe finally overplayed his hand in the move that would have paved the way for his wife Grace’s presidential ambitions, since the military strongly opposed her candidacy. (30s02)
Sound Up Brian Raftopoulos
John: This is clearly the end of Robert Mugabe, but is it the end of Grace Mugabe?
Brian: I think for Grace Mugabe it was always going to be a problem even if Mugabe was there, whether she would take over. Because in his absence her position was going to be tenuous. But if things continue the way they are, I think that would certainly be the end of her career.
Voice
There’s no doubt that the people of Zimbabwe have been desperate for a change in leadership, but whether the current situation will actually benefit the people on the ground is in question. Derek Matyszak from the Institute for Security Studies spoke to us from Harare. (15:03)
Sound Up Derek
John: The fact that there haven’t been widespread celebrations in the streets, does that tell us something about ordinary Zimbabweans view of the former vice president?
Derek: One has to bare in mind that this is not a battle between good and evil, this is a battle between the very bad and the much worse. So although there is some euphoria on the streets, where people think we are coming to the end of the Mugabe era, we have to be aware that Emmerson Mnangagwa is not a man with good democratic credentials and neither is Constantino Chiwenga.


Voice
The army committed many atrocities on behalf of it’s leaders. This veteran lived the horror. (07s04)
Sound Up “Stephen” Hidden Identity
When they gave you commands to burn the place, to kill people, I was part of that. To show the next person if you try to oppose the party, it’s you next.
Voice
Former Minister of Education in the Mugabe cabinet, David Coltart, who spoke to us telephonically from Bulawayo, is not convinced a Mnangagwa regime will do any better. (12s04f)
Sound Up David Coltart
Emmerson Mnangagwa and the military have been the same people responsible for gross human rights violations in the past, responsible for the violence in the 2008 election, and the military did all the organization on ZANU-PF’s behalf in 2013.
Voice
While his country burned, Mugabe often played the role of freedom fighter in public, battling evil western imperialists. (07s21f)
Sound Up Brian Raftopoulos
John: The narrative has changed completely, this isn’t the CIA or MI6 knocking on Mugabe’s door, it’s his own army?
Brian: Precisely, that outward mobilization of politics, that externalization of the problem, has come very much now to his doorstep. And the politics is about the unresolved issues of succession within his own party. And the manner in which they have blocked political transition from opposition over the last 37 years. And this is an outcome of those blockages.
Voice
It remains to be seen just how much influence the SADC nations can exert on the Zimbabwean military. This weeks’ emergency meeting by the Troika only led to the calling of an Extra-Ordinary SADC summit to tackle the Zimbabwean crisis. (14S14f)

Sound Up Kevin
All the multi-lateral organizations, whether it’s SADC or the African Union or the United Nations have made it very clear that extra-constitutional means of taking power, that is also known as a coup, are not accepted.
Voice
that’s why the Zimbabwean military have flat out denied staging a coup, despite all the evidence to the contrary. (07s14f)
Sound Up SB Moyo
To both our people, and the world beyond our borders, we wish to make it abundantly clear, that this is not a military takeover of government.
Voice
Sources have claimed negotiations in Zimbabwe have deadlocked, with Mugabe refusing to step down as President. It could be his last Ace in the deck, as it would be the only constitutionally viable way for the military to force a leadership change. (14s16f)
Sound Up Derek
And here we have something that’s looking very much like a coup despite the fact that the military are denying that it’s a coup, and it certainly requires intervention by SADC. You should note from their statements that they haven’t condemned the actions of the military they have just said let’s have a return to constitutionality, and please follow the constitution. They’ve ignored the fact that the constitution has been brushed aside in the past few days.
Voice
On Saturday citizens finally took to the streets of Harare, in a show of solidarity with the military. And as the world eyes the unfolding situation, Zimbabweans hope their optimism will be rewarded. (12s09f)
Sound Up Brian
There’s a great deal of skepticism, they’re nervous. There’s also a sense that they want change, this is not the change that they would have wanted to see, because the military have played such a key role in bringing about the problems that we have now.
Voice
Former president Thabo Mbeki was widely criticized for his “quiet diplomacy” approach to the problems in Zimbabwe, and so far SADC doesn’t seem to be taking a much stronger stance on the current situation. Perhaps they could take some advice from Malunga’s playbook.(16s17f)

Sound Up Kevin
In future, they should strive for a Zimbabwe where institutions are strong, where you have big institutions and not big men and women.
